topIssues.title: kona-derive, kona-engine: extension points for custom derivation rules
topIssues.author: ferranbt
topIssues.body:
<!--
Need help?
Refer to our contributing guidelines for additional information about making a good issue:
https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/.github/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
<!--
A clear and concise description of what the problem is. Ex. I'm always frustrated when [...]
-->

We embed kona and need two derivation rules kona does not have, the same way reth lets a node customise its pipeline instead of forking

**Describe the solution you'd like**
<!--
A clear and concise description of what you want to happen.
-->

1. Attach data to a batch. Our batcher submissions carry per-channel data (attestations read from L1 events) that must travel with the batches decoded from that channel down to the attributes. Today `Channel`, `SingleBatch`, `SpanBatch` and `OpAttributesWithParent` have no place for it. An extension slot on attributes (an opaque `Option<Bytes>` or a generic parameter), filled by the data source and carried through the stages untouched, would do.

2. Consolidation policy. `ConsolidateTask` decides whether an unsafe block matches derived attributes. We need to ignore a class of sequencer-injected deposit txs in that comparison and to trigger a reorg from the attached data in (1). A hook on `EngineConfig`, a trait given the attributes and the block, returning match / mismatch, defaulting to today's behaviour.

Both land once for node and proof program since they live in kona-derive and kona-engine. Is this something you would take upstream?

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
<!--
A clear and concise description of any alternative solutions or features you've considered.
-->

Forking kona.

topIssues.title: kona-node-service: let an embedder drive the sequencer without the admin RPC
topIssues.author: ferranbt
topIssues.body:
<!--
Need help?
Refer to our contributing guidelines for additional information about making a good issue:
https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/.github/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
<!--
A clear and concise description of what the problem is. Ex. I'm always frustrated when [...]
-->

We embed kona-node-service in our own binary, with our own conductor in the same process. After #23881 we can pass the engine provider in. Two things still force an RPC hop to ourselves:
1. `SequencerConfig.conductor_rpc_url` → `RollupNode::start` always builds `ConductorClient::new_http`. `SequencerActor` is already generic over `Conductor`; let the config carry a `Box<dyn Conductor>` instead of a URL.
2. The `SequencerAdminCommand` sender is created in `RollupNode::start` and only given to `AdminRpc`. Expose it to the embedder, e.g. the builder takes the channel or `start` returns a handle. #23491 had this as `SequencerHandle`; just that part would do.

With those two, start/stop/commit/leader stay in-process. `AdminRpc` keeps working as one consumer of the same sender.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
<!--
A clear and concise description of what you want to happen.
-->

Entrypoints in `EngineConfig` to configure the Kona node.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Connect all the services over JSON-RPC in loopback addresses.

topIssues.title: contracts-bedrock: dispute game gas and bond sizing under Glamsterdam
topIssues.author: conr2d
topIssues.body:
On Sepolia under Glamsterdam, the receipts of the four dispute game creations I traced show 4.4–4.6 times the gas of a local Osaka replay of the same transactions. The replay (`cast run --quick`) starts from the parent block's state, so the ratio may include a pre-state difference as well as the fork rules. It also does not separate [EIP-8037](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8037) from the other repricings these transactions exercise. EIP-8037 state gas dominates, though: new accounts, code and storage slots make up 86–88% of each receipt's gas.

| Game type | Glamsterdam gas | Osaka gas (replay) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 9 `SuperFaultDisputeGame` | 2,455,999 | 532,891 |
| 1 `PermissionedDisputeGame` | 2,103,594 | 456,482 |
| 42 (Celo) | 1,749,492 | 401,050 |
| 5 `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` | 1,066,545 | 235,295 |

**Bonds.** The 12 depth-1 `move`s I traced on type 9 games cost 976,066–976,078 gas, against 254,106–254,118 in Osaka replays. The [bond incentives spec](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/blob/main/specs/fault-proof/stage-one/bond-incentives.md) set the first bond at the Fault Proof Mainnet launch, 400,000 gas at 200 gwei, at "approximately double the cost to respond at the top level". Seven type 9 factories I queried, three on mainnet (OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink) and four on Sepolia, set the root bond (`initBonds`) to 0.08 ETH, that same 400,000 gas. At 200 gwei, it is 157% of the example response's direct gas fee under Osaka (254,118 gas in replay) and 41% under Glamsterdam (976,078 gas). The bond equals the Glamsterdam response's direct gas fee at an effective 82 gwei. Mainnet dispute game creations over about a day I sampled paid 0.08–8.3 gwei. At 8.3 gwei, the example response's direct gas fee is about a tenth of the bond, so I'm not claiming a shortfall at those prices; the question is the sizing rule.

**One small fix.** `wasRespectedGameTypeWhenCreated` has a slot of its own: slot 9 in `SuperFaultDisputeGame`, slot 10 in `FaultDisputeGame` (and `PermissionedDisputeGame`, which inherits its layout). Slot 0 has room for it in both. With the flag packed there, a game created from the new implementation while its type is respected creates one slot fewer: 97,920 state gas, or 4.0% of the sampled type 9 creation and 4.7% of the type 1. Existing games keep their layout. `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` already keeps the flag in slot 0. I haven't measured the execution-gas change of a patched build.

**Questions.**
1. Is the L1 cost of dispute game creations and moves under Glamsterdam tracked anywhere? I didn't find it in the bodies of #23015 and #23811, or in the titles of the nine public sub-issues of #20151. One of those, #19380, covers the PreimageOracle's reserved gas.
2. Should the root bond, and possibly the `getRequiredBond` curve, be revisited for Glamsterdam?
3. Would a PR for the packing be welcome?

I can share the traces, the per-transaction data and the scripts.

topPRs.title: lokahi,kona-node: proof of concept for nodes following a separate interop verifier
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
**Proof of concept, not for merge.** Opened as a draft for CI feedback. Plan and progress are in #24423.

Unifying the CL and EL into one node per chain does not fit a supernode that embeds each chain's consensus node. This checks the alternative: lokahi runs as a separate interop verifier, and each chain's kona-node derives for itself and takes its safe head, finalized head and denied blocks from lokahi over RPC.

What is in here:
- lokahi: verification, invalidation and replacement, a durable store, L1 reorg handling and finality, and op-supernode's `superroot_atTimestamp` and `supernode_syncStatus` in the same wire format.
- kona-node: the authority client (one call returns an epoch, both heads and the denied blocks), block replacement, the undo when lokahi's epoch changes, op-node's handling of unsafe payloads around a denied block, and op-node's block-building RPC for the L2 test sequencer.
- op-devstack: `DEVSTACK_SUPERNODE_KIND=lokahi` runs the supernode presets on lokahi with a kona-node per chain; a preset with a sequencer, a source node and a follower per chain; a mode that runs each chain as one op-reth process with embedded kona (the commit of #24407, cherry-picked).

No effect on users: kona-node behaves as before unless `--interop.authority-rpc` is set, and lokahi is not released.

What CI should tell us: the kona-node acceptance job now runs the supernode presets on lokahi, with the op-node job on op-supernode as the control. The proofs presets run on lokahi here for the first time, so failures there are expected until they are triaged. CI has no job for the `op-reth` mode.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2*

topPRs.title: op-node,kona,op-acceptance-tests: add a derivation parity suite
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
kona-node is replacing op-node, and on some L1 data the two clients derive different safe chains, or one halts where the other continues. The data in question is batches, deposit and system config logs, and L1 block headers, plus the L2 blocks a node reads back on a reset. Until now these differences were known only from issue reports, with nothing to show which are still live. This PR adds a suite that gives both clients the same input, compares what each derives from it, and pins every difference it finds. A fix to either client then fails a test until the difference is taken off the list. `just derivation-parity-report` in `rust/kona/tests` prints how many cases each layer runs and every difference that remains.

There is no effect on users: the PR adds tests, test helpers and a local recipe. No client code changes.

Today the suite runs 130 cases: 78 agree and 52 differ, in 20 distinct ways.

<details><summary>The 20 differences</summary>

| Difference | Cases | Layers |
|---|---:|---|
| Span batch fee fields above 128 bits: kona keeps only the low 128 bits, op-node keeps the full value | 10 | vectors, proof, node |
| Span batch that fails span-batch derivation: kona drops the rest of its channel, op-node drops only that batch | 6 | vectors, proof |
| Brotli channel with a format error: kona discards the batches decoded before the error, op-node keeps them | 5 | vectors, proof |
| Span batch before Delta: kona passes it on for batch validation to drop, op-node drops it in the channel reader | 1 | vectors |
| L1-info blob base fee: kona uses built-in Cancun, Prague and Osaka blob parameters, op-node reads them from the L1 chain config | 3 | vectors |
| Pectra blob schedule override: kona drops it once L1 activates Osaka or a BPO fork, op-node applies it whatever L1 fork is active | 1 | vectors |
| Invalid Ecotone fee scalar in the system config: kona builds the L1-info deposit, op-node halts derivation | 2 | vectors |
| L1-info calldata in another fork's layout: kona decodes it, op-node rejects it | 6 | vectors |
| L1-info calldata with non-zero padding: kona ignores the padding, op-node rejects it | 3 | vectors |
| L1-info base fee above 64 bits or blob base fee above 128 bits: kona keeps only the low bits, op-node keeps the full value | 3 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited data with non-zero padding: kona halts derivation, op-node accepts the deposit | 1 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited data with an extra word after the opaque data: kona accepts the deposit, op-node halts derivation | 1 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited from or to topic with non-zero padding: kona halts derivation, op-node accepts the deposit | 2 | vectors |
| EIP-1559 params update with a zero denominator or elasticity: kona applies it, op-node rejects it | 2 | vectors |
| EIP-1559 params update with non-zero padding: kona rejects it, op-node applies it | 1 | vectors |
| ConfigUpdate log with more than three topics: kona applies it, op-node rejects it | 1 | vectors |
| ConfigUpdate type with non-zero high bytes: kona reads the low bytes and applies it, op-node rejects it | 1 | vectors |
| Pre-Holocene L2 block with non-empty extraData: kona rebuilds its system config, op-node rejects the block | 1 | vectors |
| Holocene activating in the same L1 block as an earlier fork: kona switches to the Holocene derivation stages, op-node keeps the pre-Holocene stages | 1 | proof |
| A derived payload the engine rejects near Holocene activation: kona retries the rejected payload, op-node replaces it with a deposits-only block | 1 | node |

</details>

The suite pins today's behaviour and takes no side. Where the spec decides which client is right, the fix belongs to that client. Where the spec is silent, it needs a ruling first.

The suite has three layers, and each compares a different output.

**Vectors** call one derivation step directly, in each client. op-node writes each case's input and its own output to `rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/testdata/parity_vectors.json`. kona-derive's `parity` test runs the same inputs and compares its output with op-node's. This layer finds the exact function that differs. It covers six steps:

| Step | Input | Output compared |
|---|---|---|
| Channel reader | One channel's bytes, as the channel bank hands them on, and the L1 origin's timestamp | The batches read from the channel, in order and field by field, and whether reading stops with an error |
| L1-info deposit | The system config, sequence number, L1 origin header, L2 block timestamp and L1 chain config | The encoded L1-info deposit transaction, or an error |
| L1-info decoding | The calldata of an L2 block's L1-info deposit, and the block's timestamp | The decoded fields, encoded again in the layout they were decoded from, or an error |
| Deposit log | A `TransactionDeposited` log, with its block hash and log index | The encoded deposit transaction, or an error |
| System config log | A system config, an L1 block timestamp, and a successful L1 receipt with one log | The system config after the receipt is applied |
| System config from an L2 block | An L2 block's number, timestamp, gas limit, extraData and L1-info deposit | The system config rebuilt from the block, as on a pipeline reset, or an error |

Each input also names the rollup config to use. The file stores each config once.

**Proof:** the input is crafted batch data posted to L1 in an action test, such as a span batch that raises a transaction's fee above 128 bits. op-node derives a safe chain from it in process. The output is kona-client's verdict on two claims for the L2 block at which the clients diverge. One is op-node's output root. The other is the claim for the chain kona derives: its output root, or the claim that the block cannot be derived.

**Node:** op-node and kona-node run side by side in devstack and derive from the same L1. The input is the batches posted there: the honest batcher's in the control test, crafted ones in the others. The output is the safe head each node records for an L1 block, read through `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block`. The control test compares the two nodes' whole safe head databases. This is the only layer that reaches kona-node's engine, which kona-client does not run.

Points the diff does not make obvious:
- A system config output is compared by the values derivation reads, not by how the config stores them, so that two layouts with the same values do not count as a difference. Those values are the batcher address, overhead, scalar, gas limit, EIP-1559 parameters, operator fee, minimum base fee and DA footprint gas scalar. A zero DA footprint gas scalar is read as its default. L1-info decoding compares the encoded fields rather than the calldata for the same reason.
- The Go vector test builds every case's input again and checks it against the committed file. It then runs op-node on the committed inputs and checks its outputs. The input check skips a channel case's channel bytes, so a compressor upgrade does not fail it.
- kona's output on each vector case that differs is pinned too, in `parity_kona_differences.json`. A change in *how* kona differs therefore also fails, until its description is updated.
- A crafted proof case also checks that kona-client accepts the claim of the chain kona derives. kona-host rejects any claim when the client errors, so the rejection of op-node's claim alone does not prove the chains differ.
- Each crafted case has a control that differs only by the crafted change.
- The node-layer tests start both clients themselves. They therefore skip under `DEVSTACK_L2CL_KIND=kona-node`, where they would only repeat the op-node job.

Review:
- `go-code-reviewer` (twice), `rust-code-reviewer` and `ci-config-reviewer` ran. Their findings are fixed, except those below.
- The derivation, deposit, SP1 cost and safe-head-database reviewers are not run: the diff changes no client behaviour, and adds no dependency to a guest crate.
- The security review is still owed before this leaves draft.

Deferred, as follow-ups that change code or CI outside this PR:
- **Duplicate batch-posting step:** `dsl.PostBatches` duplicates the batch-posting helper of the SDM acceptance tests, which could wrap it.
- **Copied setup:** the side-by-side system setup is copied from `safedb_parity`, and could become a preset.
- **CI routing gap:** CI runs the proof layer only when `rust/` or `op-e2e/` changes. A PR that changes only op-node's side of a difference therefore merges green, and fails on develop. The docs now say to run the recipe for such a change. Routing `op-node/rollup/` changes to the rust e2e jobs is a separate CI change.

Not covered by a case yet:
- a channel flush reaching the channel assembler (no known way to trigger it);
- the stage origin after a reset to a pre-Holocene base near genesis;
- a batcher signature that cannot be recovered, when the batcher address is zero;
- the reset walk-back channel timeout across Granite (op-node's side needs a reset, so this belongs in the node layer).

Local runs: the vectors and the Go and Rust unit tests ran on this branch. The proof and node layers passed locally, but on `op-reth-test-engine`, `kona-node` and `op-reth` binaries built from other branches, because there was no disk space to build them here. This PR's CI is their first run on binaries built from this branch.

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock: add mock ComplianceModule and Policy for the bridge-screener devnet
topPRs.author: 0xiamflux
topPRs.body:
# DO NOT MERGE
**Description**

Adds the devnet-only compliance mocks the bridge screener integrates against, so the
off-chain service can build against real addresses and the production interfaces before the
real contracts exist.

Nothing under `src/` or `snapshots/` changes beyond a 5-line interface rename. The mocks live
in `scripts/deploy/mocks/`, which keeps them clear of the `src/`-scoped interface-mirror,
snapshot and semver checks. No OPCM, op-deployer or dev-feature changes.

`DeployComplianceMocks.s.sol` deploys the mocks and points a live Portal's `bridgeHook` at the
module. The Portal already stores a hook and `initialize` already sets one, but `initialize`
is a `reinitializer` whose version the live proxy has consumed, and that version is
`immutable`. So the script clears the proxy's `_initialized` byte and re-runs `initialize`,
the same sequence OPCM uses in `OPContractsManagerUtils.upgrade`.

A `useMockPortal` flag decides what the Portal is left running:

- **false**: re-installs the implementation the Portal already had, reading every value passed
  back to `initialize` off the Portal first, so the call changes nothing but the hook. The only
  effect on the chain is that the module joins the Portal's unsafe-target set.
- **true**: installs `MockOptimismPortal2`, which screens deposits and withdrawals through the
  hook, so the whole flow works before #23736 and the withdrawal path land. Its storage mirrors
  the real Portal's slot for slot, with a spacer for every field it does not use, so the swap
  preserves live state and is reversible. Set it false once the real paths are in.

**Tests**

`MockPolicy`: the three screening outcomes, override precedence over the per-direction
defaults, completion vs withdrawal dispatch, clearance expiry, the clear and revoke write
path, owner gating.

`MockComplianceModule`: hook entry points gated on both the caller and still being the
Portal's hook, `Held` carrying a preimage that round-trips through `hashItem`, policy-only
verdicts, the record deleted before calling out (including a re-entering policy), the disable
switch respecting the L2 nonce cutoff.

`MockOptimismPortal2`: deposit and withdrawal screening, holds emitting no
`TransactionDeposited` / `WithdrawalFinalized`, completion on committed terms, the deposit
counter distinguishing otherwise identical deposits.

`DeployComplianceMocks`: runs against a full stack. Asserts the Portal's initialized byte is
back to 4, its configuration and `l2Sender` are unchanged, and an ordinary deposit still works.
With the mock installed, asserts it reads `SystemConfig`, `AnchorStateRegistry`, `ETHLockbox`,
the maturity delay and `l2Sender` back at the live values, which is what the storage padding
exists to guarantee. A second run is refused.

162 tests pass.

**Notes for review**

- The `expiresAt` rename in the first commit follows `flux/compliance-specs`. specs#977 landed
  upstream keeping `clearedAt`, so that one is unsettled and worth a decision.
- `ItemObserved` on the Policy is mock-only. A deposit that proceeds leaves no on-chain record
  of its item ID, since `TransactionDeposited` does not carry the deposit counter.
- The script requires the L1 ProxyAdmin owner to be the broadcaster, so a multisig PAO will not
  work with it as written.
- `scripts/deploy/mocks/README.md` is the integration contract for the screener.

**Metadata**

- Part of ethereum-optimism/optimism-private#842

topPRs.title: op-chain-ops: add SDM RPC replay checks to check-lagoon
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
Adds read-only SDM RPC validation through `check-lagoon sdm rpc`, with opt-in checks for existing workflows via `--sdm.check-rpc`. Covers debug/parity replay, call-many, transaction-boundary roots, `traceChain`, JS, OTS, and raw/bad-block diagnostics against canonical receipts and state.

JS runs when available; its explicit disabled-tracer response is skipped unless `--sdm.rpc-js` requires it. OTS calls are skipped unless `--sdm.rpc-ots` is set. Unexpected errors and incorrect results still fail. JSON reports distinguish failures from skips; missing fixtures or optional skips leave `complete: false` without failing otherwise successful checks.

Targeted race tests, vet, custom lint, and the op-geth ratchet pass. Default and explicit-required modes were exercised against premium and stock nodes. This is replay-focused coverage, not every RPC/tracer option. Independent review, full-repository lint, and an end-to-end pass against settled-replay release artifacts remain pending.

topPRs.title: docs/public-docs: run the docs preview and tooling on mise-pinned bun
topPRs.author: pauldowman
topPRs.body:
Previewing docs.optimism.io locally needed Node, pnpm and a globally installed `mint` CLI, none of which the repo pins. The documented `pnpm dev` failed out of the box, and `pnpm install` itself failed under the pinned pnpm because of a placeholder `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. `just public-docs` now installs dependencies and serves the preview using only the `bun` and `just` pinned in `mise.toml`, and the generators and lints run on the same `bun`.

- **Effect on contributors:** `pnpm …` commands become `bun run …`, and Node, pnpm and tsx are no longer needed. No effect on the published site: Mintlify deploys through its GitHub app and doesn't run `package.json` scripts, and no CI job installs the docs' JS dependencies.
- **`mint` is an exact-pinned devDependency** of `docs/public-docs`, so `bun.lock` locks its whole dependency tree, rather than pinning a `bunx mint@<version>` call in the root justfile.
- **More advisories become visible; the risk is not new.** `bun audit` on the docs package goes from 8 to 43 advisories, almost all in versions that `mint` pins exactly. Contributors already ran these same packages through a global `mint` install or `npx`; the repo just had no record of them, so nothing could flag them. Exposure is a localhost preview, and the fix is bumping `mint`, which Renovate can now see (expect frequent `mint` bump PRs). `sharp` is overridden to 0.35.5 because `mint` pins the vulnerable 0.33.5, restoring the protection #22733 added.
- **`react`/`react-dom` removed:** they were unused (Mintlify supplies React at runtime; `components/HomeCard.tsx` only imports types), and their React 18 was loaded instead of `mint`'s React 19, which crashed `mint dev`.
- **Accepted:** the existing `minimatch >=9.0.7` override forces minimatch 10 onto Spectral, a `mint` dependency expecting ^3. Spectral only reaches that code for rulesets with `overrides`, and this site has no OpenAPI or AsyncAPI specs.
- Tutorials that tell readers to use pnpm, npx or tsx for their own projects are unchanged.
- `lint:nav` (887 errors) and `lint:reference` (3 errors) fail identically on `develop`; not addressed here.

Reviews: `ci-config-reviewer` and `deletion-reviewer` ran on the branch; their findings are fixed. `/op:security-reviewer` has not run yet and must run before this is marked ready. Unconfirmed: whether GitHub's dependency graph and the `dependency-review` check parse `bun.lock`.
